---
title: "Quiz: active shape models"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. One ASM iteration: suggest points along the normals, fit the pose, project onto the modes, clamp.

---

**Q1.** Which step of an ASM iteration is "a snake without internal forces", and which steps replace $\alpha$ and $\beta$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The suggestion step: every landmark moves towards a better image position on its own. Fitting the pose, projecting onto the modes and clamping replace the smoothness terms: instead of "be smooth", the points must form a shape like the training shapes.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why does the search look along the **normal** of the outline, not in every direction?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Along the outline the image hardly changes, so a move along it cannot be judged from the image; across it (along the normal) the edge is visible. Searching only along the normal also makes the search one-dimensional and cheap. Sliding along the outline is left to the shape model (which is why landmarks can end up slightly shifted along a smooth outline).
:::

---

**Q3.** The profile model at a landmark expects a dark-to-bright step. Along the normal there is a strong bright-to-dark edge 4 pixels out and a weaker dark-to-bright edge 1 pixel in. Which does each matching rule choose?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The strongest edge (by magnitude) chooses the strong edge 4 pixels out, although it has the wrong polarity. The profile model (Mahalanobis distance to the trained profile) chooses the weaker edge 1 pixel in, whose profile looks like the trained one.
:::

---

**Q4.** After projection, $b_2 = 5\sqrt{\lambda_2}$. What happens in the clamp step, and why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$b_2$ is set to $3\sqrt{\lambda_2}$: 5 standard deviations is far outside the range of the training shapes, so the suggested points are more likely wrong than the shape is real. The clamp keeps the shape plausible.
:::

---

**Q5.** Part of the object is hidden behind another object. Why can an ASM still give a sensible outline there, and a snake not?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The ASM fits pose and a few mode parameters to all landmarks at once; the visible ones determine them, and the model draws the hidden part as the training shapes look there. A snake only knows "smooth": it either follows the occluder's edge or bridges the gap with a smooth curve that has nothing to do with the object.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why does searching first on a coarse pyramid level increase the capture range?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On a level halved twice, a search of $m$ pixels covers $4m$ full-size pixels, and the blurred image has broad edges that are visible from further away. The coarse level finds the rough pose and shape; the finer levels refine it. It is also faster: few pixels, few iterations.
:::

---

**Q7.** You need to outline cells of an unusual mutant whose shapes are not in your training set. Snake or ASM?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A snake (or retrain the shape model with the mutants). The ASM can only produce shapes like its training shapes and will force the mutant's outline towards a normal cell; the snake follows whatever edge it is near.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Why is the Mahalanobis distance to the mean profile a sensible matching cost?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If the training profiles at a landmark are modelled as Gaussian $\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf g}, S)$, then $-2\log p(\mathbf g) = (\mathbf g - \bar{\mathbf g})^\top S^{-1}(\mathbf g - \bar{\mathbf g}) + $ const: the smallest distance is the most probable profile. It also weighs each sample by how much it varied in training, unlike a plain sum of squared differences.
:::
